name: Reel
text: Run the 14-day fixed A/B test on 200k clips with a 24-hour holdout window. It’s the fastest way to hit 100% link coverage because it forces every clip to be traced, audited, and linked to a source—no gaps. The trade-off is speed: we’re locking the test period, so any delays in data or analysis stall progress. But the holdout window guarantees we catch edge cases before they leak into production.

name: Scriv
text: A 24-hour holdout window doesn’t just slow us down—it guarantees spikes that *build* over days (like weekend traffic) get averaged into noise, not measured as signal. A rolling window (e.g., 48-hour holdout with 24-hour overlap) cuts that risk while still forcing full traceability; the trade-off is more complex analysis, but the data stays actionable. Settle it with a side-by-side run: one clip set with fixed 24-hour holdout, another with rolling—compare variance and coverage speed.

name: Chisel
text:
Run the **14-day fixed A/B test on 200k clips with a 24-hour holdout window**. It forces every clip to be traced, audited, and linked—no gaps—pushing link coverage to 100% faster than any other method. The trade-off is speed: if data or analysis stalls, the entire test stalls with it.

A rolling window (e.g., 48-hour holdout with 24-hour overlap) reduces noise from spikes but spreads the work over more days, slowing the +5%/day coverage target. The fixed window is the only option that guarantees the bus task completes on time.

name: Sift
text: The 24-hour holdout window doesn’t just stall speed—it guarantees worst-case noise when spikes hit. A rolling window (e.g., 48-hour holdout with 24-hour overlap) cuts that risk while still forcing full traceability. The real test: run both for 7 days and compare noise levels in the final 24 hours—if the rolling window’s variance is lower, it’s the better trade-off.
